newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.
newsitem.headline: French court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.

text.p: A French appeals court on Wednesday ordered former cabinet minister Maurice Papon, 86, to stand trial for crimes against humanity for sending Jews from wartime France to their deaths in Nazi extermination camps.

He was only the second Frenchman to be sent to trial for such crimes and may well be the last. A lower-ranking collaborator, former militia officer Paul Touvier, was jailed for life in 1994 and died in prison this year aged 81.

Papon, who rose to be Paris police chief in the 1960s and a Gaullist budget minister in the 1970s before his World War Two role was exposed, is accused of having ordered the deportation of 1,690 Jews, including 223 children, in 1942-44 when he was secretary-general of the Bordeaux regional administration.
Most were later gassed at the Auschwitz death camp.

The Bordeaux court went further than prosecutors had sought, sending Papon to a jury trial in an assize court on charges of being an accomplice to the murder and kidnapping of 10 convoys of deportees. Prosecutors had earmarked just four convoys.
The court also approved charges that Papon was an accomplice to arbitrary arrests, the arrest of minors under 15 years old, inhuman acts and attempted illegal arrests.
"(Papon) knowingly supplied the authors of these crimes the help and assistance necessary to their preparation," it read.
The arrests of minors "were part of a concerted and systematic plan carried out for and in the name of a state enforcing a policy of ideological hegemony", it said.
Papon's lawyer immediately appealed to the Supreme Court against the ruling, which follows 15 years of procedural battle by relatives of the victims.
"After 15 years of struggle, this is a victory for the civil plaintiffs, a historic decision," lawyer Gerard Boulanger, who has campaigned for the victims' families, told reporters.
"Everything we had said has been completely vindicated by the court," said Boulanger.
The Jewish Central Consistory applauded the ruling "when themes of racial differentiation are reappearing" -- a reference to the far-right National Front saying races are unequal.

At hearings last March, the prosecutor said Papon was responsible for sending Jews on four trains which left Drancy, near Paris, for the death camps in 1942 and 1944. Lawyers for victims' relatives held him responsible for six more trains.
The prosecutor said Papon must have known about Hitler's "final solution" -- the extermination of the Jews of Europe by the Nazis -- although he had no evidence to back this.
Papon's lawyer Jean-Marc Varaut said he was bitterly disappointed by the ruling, especially since it added charges.

"If you start sending to trial all those civil servants who took part in the (wartime) Vichy administration, you devalue the charge of crime against humanity," said Varaut, who had argued Papon never followed Nazi ideology and had only obeyed orders.
An "honour jury" accepted in 1981 that Papon had joined the Resistance in 1943 but the court concluded this was not proved.

Papon enjoyed a meteoric post-war career until the satirical weekly Le Canard Enchaine revealed his wartime activities in 1981. Since then, he has benefited from delaying tactics by governments and justice officials keen to avoid a trial.
The late president Francois Mitterrand, himself a former Vichy official, sought to prevent trials for crimes against humanity because he said they undermined national unity.
His Gaullist successor Jacques Chirac last year acknowledged French state responsibility in the deportation of the Jews, the first post-war leader to do so.
